title: Security+ V7 (SY0-701) practice exam
note: Original questions written for MyNextCert from the public SY0-701 exam objectives. Not real exam questions.

q.q: After a break-in at a remote boathouse, a sector adds motion-activated floodlights, posts "Area monitored" signs, and requires a second person to escort contractors. Which pairing correctly classifies the floodlights and the escort requirement?
o: Deterrent and operational
Right. Lights that switch on discourage an intruder from continuing (deterrent), and an escort rule is carried out by people following a process (operational).
Detective and managerial
The lights don't log or report anything, so they aren't detective. An escort is done by people on the floor, not a policy-level decision, so it's operational rather than managerial.
Preventive and technical
A floodlight can't physically stop someone, and an escort isn't enforced by a system, so neither preventive nor technical fits.
Compensating and physical
Neither one is standing in for a primary control that couldn't be used. The escort is a procedure, not a physical barrier.

q.q: A legacy engineering workstation can't run the endpoint agent the command requires. The ISSM approves placing it on an isolated VLAN with strict ACLs until it's replaced. What type of control is the isolated VLAN in this case?
o: Corrective
Corrective controls restore a system after an incident, like restoring from backup. Nothing has gone wrong yet.
Compensating
Right. The required control can't be applied, so an alternative safeguard is put in place to reduce the same risk until the real fix is possible.
Directive
Directive controls tell people what to do, like a policy or a sign. A VLAN is enforced by the network, not by instructions.
Deterrent
A deterrent discourages an attacker who can see it. Segmentation works whether or not anyone knows about it.

q.q: Which of the following is a managerial control?
o: A guard who checks IDs at the gate
A guard is a person carrying out a procedure on the ground: an operational (and physical) control.
A quarterly risk assessment that sets priorities
Right. Managerial (administrative) controls are about planning and oversight: risk assessments, policies and security planning.
A firewall rule that blocks Telnet traffic
Rules enforced by a device are technical controls.
Security awareness training run by the ISSO
Training is carried out by people and is usually classed as an operational control.

q.q: An admin restores a database from last night's backup after ransomware encrypted it. The restore is best described as which control type?
o: Preventive
Preventive controls stop an incident from happening. The encryption already happened.
Detective
Detective controls identify that something happened. The restore doesn't find anything.
Corrective
Right. Corrective controls fix things after an incident and bring the system back to a known good state.
Compensating
A compensating control replaces a control that can't be used. The backup restore is the normal recovery step.

q.q: A new policy states that all removable media must be scanned at the kiosk before use on unit computers. Before any technology enforces it, the policy itself is which kind of control?
o: Directive
Right. A directive control tells people what they must or must not do. The kiosk scan that enforces it would be a separate technical control.
Detective
The policy doesn't detect anything by itself. The kiosk scan would detect malware.
Physical
A written rule has no physical form that stops anyone.
Corrective
Nothing has been fixed. The policy sets an expectation ahead of time.

q.q: A message is signed with the sender's private key. A week later the sender claims they never sent it. Which security property lets the receiver prove otherwise?
o: Confidentiality
Confidentiality keeps contents secret. A signature doesn't hide anything.
Availability
Availability is about systems and data being reachable when needed.
Non-repudiation
Right. Only the holder of the private key could have produced the signature, so the sender can't credibly deny sending it.
Authorization
Authorization decides what an authenticated user may do. It doesn't prove who sent a message.

q.q: In a Zero Trust architecture, which component evaluates a request against policy and decides whether access should be granted?
o: Policy enforcement point
The PEP is the gatekeeper that allows or blocks the connection, but it acts on a decision made elsewhere.
Policy engine
Right. The policy engine (part of the policy decision point) weighs identity, device posture and context against policy and makes the grant or deny decision.
Implicit trust zone
Zero Trust removes implicit trust zones. The area behind a PEP is still subject to policy.
Subject
The subject is the user or system asking for access, not the one deciding.

q.q: Zero Trust splits network functions into a control plane and a data plane. Which of these belongs to the data plane?
o: Adaptive identity checks that raise or lower trust
Adaptive identity is part of the control plane, which makes the access decisions.
Threat scope reduction policies
Deciding how to reduce scope is policy work on the control plane.
The policy administrator
The policy administrator sits on the control plane and tells enforcement points what to do.
The policy enforcement point that passes or blocks traffic
Right. The data plane is where traffic actually flows, and the PEP sits there opening or closing the path.

q.q: A security team deploys a fake file share full of realistic but fake personnel records, and any access to it raises an alert. What is this?
o: A honeyfile set
Right. Honeyfiles are decoy files with no real use, so any access to them is suspicious. A share of fake records is a deception control.
A DNS sinkhole
A sinkhole redirects lookups for malicious domains to a controlled address. This decoy is file-based.
Data masking
Masking hides parts of real data. These records are entirely fake and meant to be touched by an attacker.
A bastion host
A bastion host is a hardened server exposed on purpose to provide a service, not a trap.

q.q: A command compares its current controls against NIST SP 800-53 to see which required controls are missing before an inspection. What is this process called?
o: Penetration test
A pen test actively tries to exploit weaknesses. Comparing against a control list is a paper exercise.
Business impact analysis
A BIA figures out how much an outage of each function would hurt, not which controls are missing.
Gap analysis
Right. A gap analysis measures where you are against where a standard says you should be, and lists the gaps to close.
Attestation
Attestation is a formal statement that controls are in place, usually after an audit, not the search for what's missing.

q.q: Which of these best describes accounting in AAA?
o: Proving a user is who they claim to be
That's authentication.
Deciding which resources a user may access
That's authorization.
Recording what users did and when
Right. Accounting tracks activity, such as logins, commands and data used, so it can be audited later.
Encrypting user sessions
Encryption protects confidentiality. It isn't one of the three A's.

q.q: A change to the cutter's firewall breaks the navigation data feed. The team restores the previous configuration within minutes. Which part of the change request made that quick recovery possible?
o: The impact analysis
Impact analysis predicts what the change might affect. It helps, but it isn't the step that undoes the change.
The backout plan
Right. A backout plan says exactly how to roll a change back if it fails, so recovery is fast and predictable.
The stakeholder list
Knowing who to notify doesn't restore the old configuration.
The maintenance window
The window controls when the change happens, not how to reverse it.

q.q: An admin patches a mail server outside the approved maintenance window, without a change ticket, because "it was a small fix." The patch restarts a dependent service and email is down for two hours. Which change management element would most directly have prevented the outage?
o: Updating the network diagram after the patch
Documentation updates matter, but doing them afterward doesn't prevent the outage.
Testing and reviewing dependencies before approval
Right. Change review catches dependent services, and testing shows the impact before production.
Notifying users after the patch is installed
Notice after the fact doesn't prevent the outage.
Scanning the server for vulnerabilities first
A scan finds weaknesses, not what a patch will break.

q.q: Before a scheduled upgrade to an application, the change board asks the team to confirm which legacy systems depend on it. Why does change management care about legacy dependencies?
o: Legacy systems are exempt from change control
Legacy systems aren't exempt. They usually need extra care because they can't be patched easily.
Older systems may break when something they rely on changes
Right. Dependencies are a classic cause of surprise outages, and legacy systems are often the most fragile.
Legacy systems set the length of every maintenance window
The organization sets windows. Legacy systems don't set them.
Legacy systems must be retired before any change
Changes happen around legacy systems all the time. They just need checking.

q.q: A unit stores user passwords as SHA-256 hashes. An attacker who steals the table finds that several users have the same hash. Which change would most directly stop identical passwords from producing identical hashes?
o: Encrypt the whole table with AES-256
Encryption protects the table at rest, but once decrypted the identical hashes are still identical.
Add a unique random salt to each password
Right. A per-user salt makes every hash different even when passwords match, and it defeats rainbow tables.
Hash each password twice with SHA-256
Double hashing without a salt still gives identical results for identical passwords.
Require users to change passwords every 30 days
Rotation doesn't stop two users from choosing the same password.

q.q: Which device is built into a laptop's motherboard to store encryption keys and check the boot process, and is what BitLocker uses to protect the drive key?
o: HSM
A hardware security module is a separate, often rack-mounted or network device for managing many keys at scale.
TPM
Right. The Trusted Platform Module is a chip on the motherboard that stores keys and measures the boot process.
Key escrow
Key escrow is a process of storing keys with a trusted third party, not a chip.
Secure enclave in a cloud provider
That's a cloud service, not part of the laptop.

q.q: A browser checks whether a website's certificate has been revoked by asking the CA's server about that one certificate, instead of downloading a full list. What is it using?
o: CRL
A certificate revocation list is the full list the browser would have to download.
CSR
A certificate signing request is what you send to a CA to get a certificate.
OCSP
Right. The Online Certificate Status Protocol checks a single certificate's status in real time.
Key stretching
Key stretching strengthens weak passwords against cracking. It has nothing to do with revocation.

q.q: A user signs an email with their private key and encrypts it with the recipient's public key. What does the recipient use to read the message and to verify the signature?
o: Their own private key to decrypt; the sender's public key to verify
Right. Only the recipient's private key unlocks what was encrypted with their public key, and the sender's public key checks the signature made with the sender's private key.
The sender's private key to decrypt; their own public key to verify
The recipient never has the sender's private key. Private keys are never shared.
Their own public key for both
A public key can't decrypt what was encrypted with that same public key.
A shared symmetric key for both
The scenario uses asymmetric keys. A symmetric key would need to be shared ahead of time.

q.q: A web server certificate needs to cover www.example.mil, mail.example.mil and portal.example.mil, and nothing else. Which certificate feature fits best?
o: A wildcard certificate for *.example.mil
A wildcard covers every first-level subdomain, which is more than the three names required.
Subject Alternative Name entries for the three names
Right. SAN lists exactly which names the certificate is valid for, so it covers these three and nothing more.
A self-signed certificate
Self-signed certificates aren't trusted by browsers and don't change which names are covered.
A code-signing certificate
Code-signing certificates sign software, not websites.

q.q: A developer needs to store customer card numbers so the payment system can still match them, but analysts should only ever see a stand-in value that can't be reversed mathematically. Which technique fits?
o: Hashing
Hashing is one-way, but the same card number always gives the same hash, and card numbers are short enough to brute-force.
Tokenization
Right. Tokenization swaps the real value for a random token and keeps the mapping in a secure vault, so the token can't be reversed with math.
Obfuscation
Obfuscation just makes something harder to read. It isn't a protection you can rely on.
Steganography
Steganography hides data inside other data, like an image. It doesn't replace values.

q.q: Which TWO statements about symmetric and asymmetric encryption are correct? (Choose two.)
o: Symmetric encryption is much faster, so it is used for bulk data
Right. Symmetric ciphers such as AES are fast, so they encrypt the actual data.
Asymmetric encryption is commonly used to exchange the symmetric session key
Right. Protocols like TLS use asymmetric cryptography to agree on or protect a symmetric session key.
Symmetric encryption uses a public and a private key
That describes asymmetric encryption. Symmetric uses one shared key.
Asymmetric encryption needs shorter keys than symmetric for the same strength
It's the reverse: RSA needs much longer keys than AES for comparable strength.
Asymmetric encryption removes the need for certificates
Certificates are how people trust that a public key belongs to someone.

q.q: A well-funded group quietly keeps access to a defense contractor's network for 14 months, steals design files, and uses custom malware that no antivirus vendor has seen. Which threat actor is most likely?
o: Hacktivist
Hacktivists want attention for a cause, so they usually deface or leak loudly rather than hide for over a year.
Unskilled attacker
Custom malware and long-term stealth take skill and money an unskilled attacker doesn't have.
Nation-state
Right. Long dwell time, custom tools and espionage against defense targets are classic signs of a nation-state (advanced persistent threat).
Organized crime
Criminal groups want money fast, for example through ransomware or fraud, rather than quiet theft of design files.

q.q: An employee who was passed over for promotion copies the unit's contact roster to a personal cloud account before transferring. What is the best description of this threat?
o: Insider threat motivated by revenge
Right. The person had legitimate access, and the grievance points to revenge as the motive.
Shadow IT
Shadow IT is using unapproved technology to get work done. This is deliberate data theft.
Nation-state espionage
Nothing here points to a foreign government.
Unskilled attacker using purchased tools
Copying files you already have access to isn't an outside attack.

q.q: A department buys a free online project tracker and puts unit schedules in it without telling IT. What is this an example of?
o: Shadow IT
Right. Shadow IT is technology used without IT's knowledge or approval, which leaves data outside the organization's controls.
Supply chain attack
No supplier was compromised. The department chose the tool itself.
Insider threat
There's no malicious intent; the people just wanted a tool that worked.
Watering hole attack
A watering hole compromises a site the victims visit. Nothing was compromised here.

q.q: Which attribute most clearly separates a nation-state actor from an unskilled attacker?
o: Location outside the country
Unskilled attackers can be anywhere too. Location alone doesn't separate them.
Level of resources and funding
Right. Nation-states have large budgets, staff and time, which shows in their tools and persistence.
Use of email as a vector
Both use email. Phishing is common to almost every actor.
Whether they target home users
Both can hit anyone. Targeting isn't the defining difference.

q.q: A group floods a city's emergency services website with traffic during a protest and posts a statement about the cause it supports. What is the most likely motivation?
o: Financial gain from a ransom demand
No payment was demanded.
Philosophical or political beliefs
Right. Publicly tying the attack to a cause is the signature of a hacktivist.
Espionage to steal emergency plans
Espionage is quiet. A loud DDoS with a public statement is the opposite.
Revenge by a former city employee
Nothing points to an insider grievance. The statement is about a cause.

q.q: Several sailors receive a text that appears to come from the Coast Guard Mutual Assistance office, asking them to "confirm their account" through a link. What is this attack?
o: Vishing
Vishing is voice phishing over a phone call.
Smishing
Right. Smishing is phishing by SMS text message.
Pharming
Pharming redirects users to a fake site by tampering with DNS or hosts files, without needing them to click a link.
Whaling
Whaling targets senior executives specifically, not a group of junior members.

q.q: Attackers compromise a website that members of a particular cutter community visit often, and plant malware there to infect those visitors. What is this called?
o: Watering hole attack
Right. The attacker poisons a site the target group already trusts and visits, then waits for them to come.
Typosquatting
Typosquatting registers a misspelled domain, hoping people mistype the real one.
Business email compromise
BEC uses a compromised or spoofed email account to trick someone into sending money or data.
Brand impersonation
Brand impersonation copies a brand's look on a fake site or message. Here the real site was compromised.

q.q: A USB drive labeled "Bonus schedule FY27" is found in the parking lot and plugged in by curious staff. Which vector is the attacker relying on?
o: Unsecure wireless network
The attack doesn't touch Wi-Fi.
Removable media and curiosity
Right. The drive is the delivery method, and the tempting label exploits curiosity.
Malicious email attachment
Nothing arrived by email.
Compromised software update
The drive wasn't part of a vendor update.

q.q: A vendor's software update server is breached, and a signed update containing a backdoor is pushed to thousands of customers, including the unit. What is this?
o: A zero-day exploit
A zero-day uses an unknown flaw. Here the attacker abused the trusted update channel.
A supply chain attack
Right. The attacker compromised a trusted supplier so the malicious code arrives through a normal, signed update.
A brute-force attack
Nothing was guessed.
Pretexting
Pretexting is a made-up story told to a person to get information.

q.q: Which TWO actions reduce the attack surface of a new server before it goes into production? (Choose two.)
o: Disable services and ports the server doesn't need
Right. Every service that isn't running is one less way in.
Change or disable default accounts and passwords
Right. Default credentials are published online and are one of the first things attackers try.
Enable verbose error messages for troubleshooting
Detailed errors can leak information to attackers. They should be off in production.
Install the full set of optional components in case they're needed later
Extra components add attack surface without a need.
Put the server in the same subnet as user workstations
Mixing servers and workstations makes lateral movement easier, not harder.

q.q: An attacker calls the help desk pretending to be a commanding officer who's locked out before a briefing and demands an immediate password reset. Which two principles of social engineering is the caller using most?
o: Authority and urgency
Right. Claiming high rank and a time crunch pressures the help desk to skip the normal identity checks.
Scarcity and familiarity
Nothing is in limited supply, and the caller isn't building rapport.
Consensus and trust
The caller doesn't claim that everyone else is doing it.
Intimidation and scarcity
There's some intimidation, but scarcity isn't part of it. Authority and urgency fit better.

q.q: A web form builds its database query like this. Which vulnerability does this create?
o: Cross-site scripting
XSS injects script into pages viewed by other users. This input goes into a database query.
SQL injection
Right. Concatenating raw input into SQL lets an attacker change the query, for example with ' OR '1'='1. Parameterized queries fix it.
Buffer overflow
A buffer overflow writes past the end of a memory buffer. This is a query-building flaw.
Race condition
A race condition depends on timing between two operations. Timing doesn't matter here.
q.code: query = "SELECT * FROM members WHERE emplid = '" + userInput + "';"

q.q: A program checks that a file belongs to the user, and then a fraction of a second later opens it. An attacker swaps the file for a link to a system file between those two steps. What type of vulnerability is this?
o: Memory injection
No code is injected into memory.
Race condition (TOCTOU)
Right. The file checked at one moment was swapped before it was used: a time-of-check to time-of-use race condition.
Directory traversal
Traversal uses ../ in a path to escape a folder. Here the file itself is swapped.
Privilege escalation through a buffer overflow
No memory is overflowed. The flaw is about timing between two steps.

q.q: A security researcher finds a flaw in a firewall model that the vendor doesn't know about, and no patch exists. What is this called?
o: A misconfiguration
A misconfiguration is a setting someone got wrong, not a flaw in the product's code.
An end-of-life vulnerability
End of life means the vendor stopped supporting the product. The problem here is that no one knows about the flaw yet.
A zero-day vulnerability
Right. A zero-day is unknown to the vendor, so it has zero days of patch available.
A known exploited vulnerability
KEV entries are flaws that are known and actively exploited.

q.q: An attacker who controls one virtual machine on a host manages to run code on the hypervisor and reach the other VMs. What is this called?
o: VM escape
Right. Breaking out of a guest VM to the hypervisor is VM escape, the worst case in virtualization.
VM sprawl
VM sprawl is having too many unmanaged VMs. It's a management problem, not an exploit.
Resource reuse
Resource reuse is when leftover data in reassigned memory or storage leaks between tenants.
Jailbreaking
Jailbreaking removes restrictions from a mobile device's OS.

q.q: A sailor installs an app from a website instead of the official app store because it isn't available there. What is this, and what is the main risk?
o: Sideloading; the app hasn't been vetted by the store and may be malicious
Right. Sideloading skips the app store's review, so malware is much more likely.
Rooting; the device's operating system loses its update channel
Rooting gives the user administrator access to Android. Installing one outside app doesn't root the phone.
Tethering; the phone's data plan can be used by attackers
Tethering shares the phone's connection with other devices.
Carrier unlocking; the phone can be moved to another carrier
Unlocking is about which networks the phone can use.

q.q: An S3 bucket holding a unit's training records is set so anyone on the internet can list and download its files. Which category of vulnerability is this?
o: Zero-day
Nothing about the cloud service itself is broken.
Misconfiguration
Right. The service works as designed; someone set its permissions wrong. Misconfiguration is the leading cause of cloud data exposure.
Cryptographic
The issue isn't weak encryption but public access.
Supply chain
No supplier was compromised.

q.q: The SIEM shows one account authenticating from Norfolk, Virginia at 0902 and from an overseas IP at 0911 the same morning. Which indicator is this?
o: Resource consumption
Resource consumption is about unusual CPU, disk or bandwidth use.
Impossible travel
Right. Nobody can travel that far in nine minutes, so the credentials are probably being used by someone else.
Account lockout
Nothing was locked out.
Blocked content
Nothing was blocked.

q.q: Users report their files now have a .locked extension, and a text file on every share demands payment in cryptocurrency. What malware is this?
o: Spyware
Spyware quietly watches users. It doesn't announce itself or demand payment.
Ransomware
Right. Encrypting files and demanding payment for the key is ransomware.
Logic bomb
A logic bomb runs when a condition is met, like a date, but doesn't by nature demand payment.
Rootkit
A rootkit hides deep in the OS to keep an attacker's access. It doesn't encrypt files.

q.q: A domain admin's account logs into dozens of servers in five minutes at 0300 using an NTLM hash, without a password being typed. Which attack does this suggest?
o: Pass-the-hash
Right. Pass-the-hash reuses a stolen NTLM hash to authenticate without knowing the password, and rapid logins across servers show lateral movement.
Password spraying
Spraying tries one common password against many accounts. This is one account using a hash.
Birthday attack
A birthday attack looks for hash collisions. It isn't used to log in.
Downgrade attack
A downgrade forces weaker protocol versions. Nothing here is negotiated down.

q.q: A web server log shows this request. What is the attacker attempting?
o: Directory traversal
Right. The ../ sequences try to climb out of the web root to read files like /etc/passwd.
Cross-site request forgery
CSRF tricks a logged-in user's browser into sending a request. This request comes directly from the attacker.
Command injection
Command injection adds OS commands such as ; or && to input. This uses path sequences.
Replay attack
A replay resends captured traffic. This is a new crafted request.

q.q: During an outage the network team sees that the default gateway's IP address keeps switching between two different MAC addresses on the LAN. What is the most likely attack?
o: DNS cache poisoning
DNS poisoning corrupts name lookups. The problem here is IP-to-MAC mapping on the LAN.
ARP poisoning
Right. An attacker answering ARP for the gateway's IP puts themselves between hosts and the gateway (an on-path attack).
MAC flooding of the switch
MAC flooding fills a switch's table with fake addresses. It doesn't make one IP map to a new MAC.
A rogue DHCP server
A rogue DHCP server hands out bad settings, but wouldn't make the gateway's IP flip between two MACs.

q.q: Over a weekend, the authentication logs show one failed login for each of 300 different accounts, all from the same IP, all using the password "Winter2026!". What is this?
o: Brute force
Brute force hammers one account with many passwords.
Password spraying
Right. One common password tried once against many accounts avoids lockouts. That's spraying.
Credential stuffing
Credential stuffing reuses username and password pairs leaked from other sites, usually different for each account.
Dictionary attack against one user
This targets many users, not one.

q.q: A user's browser is sending requests to the bank site whenever they visit a forum, because the forum embeds a hidden form that posts to the bank using the user's logged-in session. What is this?
o: Cross-site request forgery (CSRF)
Right. CSRF makes a logged-in user's browser send an unwanted request that the bank trusts because of the session cookie.
Stored cross-site scripting
Stored XSS runs attacker script on the vulnerable site itself. Here the forum just sends a forged request to another site.
Session replay
Replay resends captured traffic later. Here a new request is made in real time.
Clickjacking
Clickjacking hides a real page under a fake button to steal clicks. No click on a hidden page is described.

q.q: Which TWO findings most strongly suggest a host is part of a botnet? (Choose two.)
o: Regular outbound connections every 60 seconds to the same unknown domain
Right. Steady, periodic check-ins (beaconing) to an unknown host are a classic command-and-control pattern.
Large bursts of outbound traffic to many targets at once during an attack window
Right. A botnet member sends attack traffic, such as a DDoS, when commanded.
A Windows update downloading from Microsoft
Updates from the vendor are normal.
A user streaming a training video
Ordinary streaming isn't an indicator of compromise.
The antivirus signature file updating overnight
Signature updates are expected and healthy.

q.q: A command wants only approved programs to run on its kiosk PCs, no matter what a user downloads. Which mitigation is the best fit?
o: Application allow list
Right. An allow list (whitelist) blocks every program that isn't explicitly approved.
Block list of known malware
A block list only stops known bad programs, so anything new still runs.
Disk encryption
Encryption protects data at rest, not which programs run.
Port security
Port security limits which devices can use a switch port.

q.q: After a phishing compromise of one workstation, the attacker moved to the HR file server and the industrial control network. Which mitigation would have done most to limit that spread?
o: Stronger passwords on every workstation
The attacker came in by phishing and moved laterally. Longer passwords don't block that path.
Network segmentation with access controls
Right. Segmentation keeps one compromised host from reaching unrelated networks such as HR or ICS.
Full-disk encryption on the workstation
Disk encryption protects a stolen device, not a running one under attacker control.
Longer log retention on the file server
Retention helps investigations later but doesn't stop movement.

q.q: Admins currently use their domain admin accounts to read email. What does the principle of least privilege suggest?
o: Give the admin account MFA and keep using it for email
MFA helps, but a phishing payload would still run with domain admin rights.
Use a standard account daily and the admin account only for admin work
Right. If a phishing email hits a standard account, the attacker doesn't get domain admin rights.
Block external email for every admin account
That cuts one risk but admin rights stay in daily use for everything else.
Rotate the admin password every day automatically
Rotation doesn't stop an attacker who already has a live session.

q.q: A vulnerability scan flags an OS flaw on a server that can't be patched for 30 days because of an operational freeze. Which TWO actions are the best interim mitigations? (Choose two.)
o: Restrict network access to the server to only the systems that need it
Right. Limiting who can reach the vulnerable service reduces the chance it can be exploited.
Increase monitoring and alerting on that server
Right. If it can't be fixed yet, watch it closely so exploitation is caught fast.
Mark the finding as a false positive
It isn't a false positive, and hiding it removes it from tracking.
Turn off logging to improve performance
Less logging means less chance of detecting an attack.
Disable the host firewall so the patch installs smoothly later
That increases exposure while the flaw is still open.

q.q: Which hardening step addresses the risk of attackers using a workstation's open but unused services?
o: Disabling unnecessary ports and protocols
Right. Shutting off what isn't needed removes those ways in.
Installing a host-based firewall and allowing all inbound traffic
A firewall that allows everything doesn't reduce exposure.
Encrypting the hard drive
Encryption doesn't close network services.
Enabling auto-login for convenience
Auto-login weakens security.

q.q: A command wants to stop a compromised laptop from talking to anything except the remediation server while IR works on it. What is this mitigation called?
o: Isolation
Right. Isolating the host cuts off its access to everything but what responders allow.
Decommissioning
Decommissioning retires an asset permanently.
Configuration enforcement
That applies standard settings to devices, but doesn't cut off a compromised host.
Patching
Patching fixes a known flaw. It doesn't contain an active compromise.

q.q: Under the cloud shared responsibility model, who is responsible for patching the guest operating system on an IaaS virtual machine?
o: The cloud provider
In IaaS the provider secures the physical hosts, network and hypervisor. The guest OS is yours.
The customer
Right. In IaaS you manage the operating system and everything above it: patches, configuration, applications and data.
Both share it equally
Responsibilities are split by layer, not shared equally. The guest OS sits on the customer's side.
Nobody, because cloud VMs patch themselves
IaaS VMs don't patch themselves unless you set that up.

q.q: A team defines its servers, networks and firewall rules in Terraform files that are reviewed and version-controlled before deployment. What is the main security benefit?
o: It removes the need for access control on the account
Access control still matters, especially to the pipeline that deploys the code.
Consistent, reviewed and repeatable configurations
Right. Infrastructure as Code means every change is reviewed and every deployment matches the approved definition, which reduces drift.
It encrypts all deployed data by default
IaC describes infrastructure. Encryption is only on if the code turns it on.
It patches the servers' operating systems automatically
IaC deploys what you define. It doesn't patch the OS by itself.

q.q: A water treatment plant's control network uses PLCs that can't be patched and run 24/7. What is the most appropriate protection?
o: Patch the PLCs monthly with the rest of the IT systems
These controllers often can't be patched without stopping the process, and many have no patches at all.
Segment the ICS network and tightly control what can reach it
Right. Isolation and strict access control are the main defenses for ICS/SCADA systems that can't be updated like normal IT.
Connect the PLCs directly to the internet for remote vendor support
Direct internet exposure of ICS is a well-known path to attacks.
Install the same desktop antivirus used on workstations
Desktop antivirus usually can't run on PLCs.

q.q: An application is split into many small services that talk over APIs, and each runs in its own container. Which security concern grows the most with this design?
o: Each container needs its own physical server
Containers share a host. They don't each need a server.
More service-to-service APIs that must be secured
Right. Splitting an app into many services adds endpoints and connections, so the internal attack surface grows.
Users must sign in once for every microservice
SSO and tokens let users sign in once. The concern is the service-to-service traffic.
Encryption can no longer be used between services
Services can and should use TLS (often mutual TLS) between them.

q.q: A small embedded device in a buoy runs a real-time operating system with very limited CPU and memory. Which constraint most often limits the security controls you can add to it?
o: Its long battery life makes logging unnecessary
Battery life doesn't make logging unnecessary, and constrained devices usually have the opposite problem.
Limited compute power, which may rule out heavy agents
Right. Constrained devices often can't run security agents or strong cryptography, so they rely on network protections.
A real-time OS can't use any network at all
Embedded devices are often networked. That's part of their risk.
It must store all its data in a public cloud
Embedded systems don't require cloud storage.

q.q: A unit moves an app to a serverless platform where the provider runs the code only when a function is called. What does the unit still have to secure?
o: The underlying servers and their OS patches
In serverless, the provider manages the servers and OS.
The function code, its permissions and data
Right. With serverless you don't manage servers, but your code, its access rights and your data are still yours to secure.
The hypervisor that isolates each function
The hypervisor is the provider's responsibility.
The physical security of the provider's data center
The provider secures its data centers.

q.q: Where should a public-facing web server be placed so that, if compromised, it can't reach the internal network directly?
o: On the internal LAN, behind the perimeter firewall
That puts a high-risk, internet-facing system right next to sensitive internal assets.
In a screened subnet (DMZ) between firewall zones
Right. A DMZ lets the internet reach the server while firewall rules stop the server from opening connections inward.
On the management VLAN with the network devices
Management networks should be the most restricted, never public-facing.
In front of the firewall, directly on the internet
With nothing in front of it, the server takes every attack and isn't separated from anything.

q.q: A network team wants a device that inspects traffic inline and blocks packets matching known attack signatures. Which should they deploy, and how?
o: An IDS connected to a SPAN (mirror) port
An IDS on a mirror port only sees copies of traffic, so it can alert but not block.
An IPS placed inline in the traffic path
Right. An IPS must sit in the traffic path to drop malicious packets.
An IPS connected to a SPAN (mirror) port
On a mirror port even an IPS only sees copies, so it can't drop the real packets.
An IDS placed inline in the traffic path
An IDS only alerts, wherever it sits. Blocking is what makes it an IPS.

q.q: Which control makes a switch port check a device's credentials, through RADIUS, before giving it network access?
o: Port mirroring
Mirroring copies traffic for monitoring.
Right. IEEE 802.1X is port-based network access control: the device must authenticate before the port passes traffic.
Spanning Tree Protocol
STP prevents switching loops.
VLAN trunking
Trunking carries multiple VLANs on one link.

q.q: Remote users need access to one internal web app without being placed on the internal network, and each request should be checked against identity and device posture. Which approach best fits?
o: Full-tunnel remote access VPN to the whole network
A traditional VPN puts the user on the network, which gives more access than needed.
Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA)
Right. ZTNA gives access to one application at a time after checking the user and device, instead of broad network access.
Opening the app's port to the internet
That exposes the app to everyone.
Port forwarding on the home router
Port forwarding is about the user's home network and doesn't secure the app.

q.q: A firewall rule set ends with "deny any any." What is this rule called, and where must it go?
o: Implicit deny; it must be the last rule
Right. Rules are processed top to bottom, so the catch-all deny has to come last or it blocks everything after it.
Implicit deny; it must be the first rule
As the first rule it would block all traffic before any allow rule is reached.
Stateful rule; it can go anywhere
Position matters in an ordered rule set.
Port security rule; it belongs on the switch
This is a firewall rule, not switch port security.

q.q: A command wants admins to reach servers in a secure zone only through a single hardened, monitored host. What should it deploy?
o: A jump server
Right. A jump server (jump box) is the single, controlled entry point into a secure zone, so admin access can be watched and limited.
A proxy server for user browsing
A forward proxy handles users' web traffic.
A honeypot
A honeypot is a decoy, not an access path.
A load balancer
A load balancer distributes client traffic.

q.q: Which architecture delivers networking (SD-WAN) and security services such as secure web gateway, CASB and ZTNA together as a cloud service?
o: SASE
Right. Secure Access Service Edge combines network and security functions in the cloud, close to users wherever they are.
SCADA
SCADA controls industrial processes.
NAC
Network access control checks devices before they join the LAN.
SAN
A storage area network provides block storage to servers.

q.q: A firewall is described as "fail closed." What happens if it crashes?
o: All traffic is allowed until it restarts
That's fail open.
All traffic is blocked until it restarts
Right. Fail closed favors security over availability: nothing passes when the device fails.
It switches to a backup VLAN
That describes a failover setup, not fail closed.
It sends logs to the SIEM and keeps filtering
A crashed device can't keep filtering.

q.q: Which states of data does TLS protect?
o: Data at rest
Data at rest is stored data, protected by disk or database encryption.
Data in transit
Right. TLS encrypts data as it moves across a network.
Data in use
Data in use is being processed in memory, which TLS doesn't protect.
All three states
TLS only covers data while it travels.

q.q: A help desk tool shows only the last four digits of a member's SSN, while the full number stays in the database. What technique is this?
o: Data masking
Right. Masking hides part of the data from people who don't need to see all of it.
Tokenization
Tokenization replaces the whole value with a token stored separately.
Hashing
A hash would replace the whole value with a fixed-length digest.
Geofencing
Geofencing limits access by location.

q.q: A command must keep personnel data stored inside the United States because of legal requirements. Which concept does this address?
o: Data sovereignty
Right. Data sovereignty means data is subject to the laws of the country where it's stored, so location matters.
Data masking
Masking hides data from viewers. It doesn't control where the data lives.
Data in use
That's a state of data, not a location requirement.
Data minimization
Minimization limits how much data is collected.

q.q: Which data type should get the strongest protection because its exposure would directly harm national security?
o: Public
Public data is meant to be released.
Classified
Right. Classified government data is labeled by the harm its disclosure would cause to national security.
Proprietary
Proprietary data is a company's trade secrets. It's sensitive, but national security is the higher bar.
Critical
Critical describes how important data is to operations, not its secrecy level.

q.q: Which TWO methods protect data at rest on a lost laptop? (Choose two.)
o: Full-disk encryption
Right. FDE makes the drive unreadable without the key.
Encrypting sensitive files individually
Right. File-level encryption protects specific files even if the disk is read.
TLS
TLS protects data in transit, not on the disk.
A web application firewall
A WAF protects web apps from network attacks.
Strong Wi-Fi encryption
WPA3 protects wireless traffic, not stored files.

q.q: A command wants its HR application to refuse sign-ins that come from outside the United States, even with valid credentials. Which data protection method is this?
o: Geographic restrictions
Right. Geographic restrictions (geofencing or geolocation rules) limit access based on where the request comes from.
Data masking
Masking hides part of the data a user sees. It doesn't block where they sign in from.
Hashing
Hashing creates a fixed digest of data. It doesn't control access.
Data sovereignty
Sovereignty is about the laws that apply where data is stored, not where users sign in from.

q.q: A command needs a recovery site that can take over within minutes, with live data replication and running equipment. Which site type fits?
o: Cold site
A cold site has space and power but no ready equipment, so recovery takes days or weeks.
Warm site
A warm site has some equipment but needs data restored and configuration, so recovery takes hours to days.
Hot site
Right. A hot site is fully equipped and kept in sync, so it can take over almost immediately. It's also the most expensive.
Mobile site
A mobile site is a trailer or container that has to be moved and set up first.

q.q: Backups run every night at 0200. A server fails at 1600. What is the most data the unit could lose, and which metric does that describe?
o: Up to 14 hours of data; recovery point objective (RPO)
Right. Everything since the 0200 backup could be lost. RPO is the maximum data loss, measured in time, the business accepts.
Up to 14 hours of data; recovery time objective (RTO)
RTO is how long systems can be down, not how much data is lost.
No data; backups are nightly
Changes made after 0200 aren't in last night's backup.
Up to 24 hours of data; mean time between failures (MTBF)
MTBF predicts how often a device fails.

q.q: A full backup runs Sunday. Which daily backup type lets a Thursday restore use only Sunday's full plus one other backup set?
o: Incremental
With incrementals you'd need Sunday's full plus every incremental from Monday to Thursday.
Differential
Right. Each differential holds everything changed since the last full, so you need the full plus only the latest differential.
Snapshot of the boot volume
A snapshot of one volume doesn't replace the data backup chain.
Copy backup
A copy backup doesn't reset archive bits and isn't part of the restore chain described.

q.q: Two firewalls are set up so that if the active one fails, the standby takes over within seconds. What is this?
o: Load balancing in active/active mode
Active/active shares the load at all times. This is one active and one standby.
High availability with active/passive failover
Right. Active/passive keeps a standby ready to take over when the primary fails.
Clustering for capacity planning
Capacity planning is about having enough resources, not failover.
Geographic dispersion
Geographic dispersion spreads sites apart to survive regional disasters.

q.q: A unit's data center loses commercial power. A UPS carries the load for 10 minutes. What should take over for a longer outage?
o: A second UPS of the same size
Two small UPS units still only cover a short outage.
A generator
Right. The UPS bridges the gap until the generator starts and can run for hours or days on fuel.
A power distribution unit
A PDU distributes power within a rack. It doesn't generate any.
A surge protector
A surge protector stops voltage spikes but doesn't supply power.

q.q: Which test runs real workloads at the backup site at the same time as the primary, to prove the plan works without stopping operations?
o: Tabletop exercise
A tabletop is a discussion of the plan, with no systems touched.
Parallel processing test
Right. In a parallel test the backup site runs real workloads alongside the primary, so failures don't hurt operations.
Simulation
A simulation walks through a scenario but doesn't run production on the backup site.
Full failover
A full failover switches operations away from the primary entirely, which is riskier than running in parallel.

q.q: A unit rolls out 200 new laptops. Which step should come first so every laptop starts secure and can be checked against a standard later?
o: Install every optional application users might ask for
Extra software adds attack surface.
Apply a security baseline such as a STIG image
Right. A secure baseline sets known-good settings from day one, and later scans can compare each laptop against it.
Run a vulnerability scan on one sample laptop
Scanning one laptop doesn't make the other 199 secure.
Join them to the domain before any configuration
Joining the domain is part of setup, but the secure baseline is what makes them start secure.

q.q: Which wireless setting gives a small office the strongest protection without a RADIUS server?
o: WPA2-Personal with TKIP
TKIP is outdated and weak.
WPA3-Personal using SAE
Right. WPA3-Personal uses Simultaneous Authentication of Equals, which resists offline password-guessing attacks better than WPA2's handshake.
WEP with a 128-bit key
WEP has been broken for many years.
An open network with a hidden SSID
Hiding the SSID isn't security, and an open network has no encryption.

q.q: A unit lets members use personal phones for email, but wants to wipe only work data if a phone is lost. Which mobile solution fits?
o: MDM with a full remote wipe of the device
A full wipe erases the member's personal data too.
MDM with containerization of work data
Right. A work container can be wiped on its own, leaving personal photos and apps alone.
A VPN profile pushed to the phone
A VPN protects traffic. It doesn't separate or wipe data.
Requiring a stronger screen lock PIN
A strong PIN helps, but it doesn't let the unit wipe only work data.

q.q: A developer wants to run an untrusted file to see what it does, without risking the rest of the system. What should they use?
o: Sandboxing
Right. A sandbox runs code in an isolated environment so its effects can be watched without harm.
Code signing
Code signing proves who published code. It doesn't contain untrusted code.
Input validation
Input validation checks data entered into an app.
Static code analysis
Static analysis reads source code without running it.

q.q: Old hard drives with personnel records are being retired. The unit needs proof the data can't be recovered. What should it get from the disposal vendor?
o: A certificate of destruction
Right. A certificate documents that media was destroyed or sanitized, which supports audits and compliance.
A purchase order
A purchase order proves you paid, not that data was destroyed.
A data classification label
Labels mark sensitivity but don't prove disposal.
An SLA
An SLA sets service levels. It doesn't confirm destruction.

q.q: A security team can't patch software it doesn't know exists. Which practice best addresses this?
o: Running a monthly vulnerability scan of the server subnet
A scan helps, but only on systems it knows about. Unknown assets need an inventory first.
Keeping an accurate inventory of hardware and software
Right. You can only protect what you know you have, so asset inventory comes first.
Encrypting every server that holds sensitive data
Encryption doesn't reveal what's installed.
Enabling automatic updates only on workstations
Unknown software on servers would still be missed.

q.q: Which method sanitizes an SSD so data can't be recovered, while leaving the drive reusable?
o: Degaussing
Degaussing uses a magnetic field and doesn't work on SSDs, which store data in flash memory. It also ruins magnetic drives.
Cryptographic erase or the drive's secure erase command
Right. SSDs need firmware-level secure erase or a crypto erase (destroying the encryption key). Simple overwriting can miss flash cells.
Deleting the files and emptying the recycle bin
Deleted files can usually be recovered.
Formatting the drive with a quick format
A quick format leaves the data in place.

q.q: Two findings come back from a scan: one with CVSS 9.8 on an internal lab server with no sensitive data, and one with CVSS 7.5 on the internet-facing payroll server. Which should most likely be fixed first, and why?
o: The 9.8, because CVSS alone sets the order
CVSS measures technical severity, but priority also depends on exposure and what the system holds.
The 7.5, because it's internet-facing and holds payroll data
Right. Prioritization weighs severity with exposure and asset value. An exposed, high-value system often comes first.
The 9.8, because lab servers are never segmented
Nothing says the lab server is unsegmented, and that wouldn't outweigh payroll exposure.
Neither until a pen test confirms both are exploitable
Waiting for a pen test delays fixing a known exposed flaw.

q.q: A scan reports a vulnerable Apache version on a server, but the admin confirms Apache was removed months ago and the scanner read an old banner. What is this finding?
o: False negative
A false negative is a real problem the scanner missed.
False positive
Right. The scanner reported a problem that doesn't actually exist.
True positive
A true positive is a real, confirmed problem.
True negative
A true negative is correctly reporting that there's no problem.

q.q: A scanner logs into each server with an account to check installed patches and configuration from the inside. What kind of scan is this?
o: Credentialed scan
Right. A credentialed scan has access to read patch levels and settings, so it's more accurate.
Non-credentialed scan
A non-credentialed scan only sees what's visible from the network.
Passive scan
Passive scanning only listens to traffic and doesn't log in.
Penetration test
A pen test tries to exploit weaknesses.

q.q: After a patch is applied for a critical finding, what should the team do before closing the ticket?
o: Lower the finding's severity in the tracker
Changing the severity doesn't confirm the fix.
Rescan or otherwise verify the vulnerability is gone
Right. Validation confirms the fix worked, since patches sometimes fail or need a reboot.
Ask the system owner to confirm by email
An email isn't evidence that the vulnerability is gone.
Wait for the next quarterly scan to catch it
The ticket shouldn't close on an unverified fix.

q.q: A command can't patch a vulnerable system until the vendor releases a fix, so the risk owner formally signs off on running it as is for 60 days with monitoring. What is this called?
o: Risk transference to the vendor until the patch ships
Transference moves the risk to another party, such as an insurer. The command is keeping the risk.
An exception with documented risk acceptance
Right. When a fix isn't possible yet, the risk is formally accepted for a set time, documented and reviewed.
Compensating control approval for the vendor's code
A compensating control would be an added safeguard. The sign-off described is the acceptance itself.
Risk avoidance by keeping the system in service
Avoidance would mean stopping the activity, which is the opposite of what's described.

q.q: Which tool collects logs from firewalls, servers and endpoints, correlates related events and raises alerts in one place?
o: SIEM
Right. A Security Information and Event Management system aggregates and correlates logs and alerts on suspicious patterns.
NetFlow collector
NetFlow shows who talked to whom and how much, but not full logs from every source.
Vulnerability scanner
A scanner finds weaknesses but doesn't correlate live events.
DLP
DLP watches for sensitive data leaving.

q.q: The SOC is getting hundreds of low-value alerts a day and is starting to ignore them. What should the team do?
o: Raise every alert to critical so none are missed
If everything is critical, nothing stands out.
Tune the rules to cut false positives and set priorities
Right. Tuning cuts noise so real alerts get attention, which fights alert fatigue.
Send all low-severity alerts to a shared mailbox
That just moves the noise somewhere nobody reads.
Shorten log retention so the SIEM has less data
Less retained data doesn't reduce noisy alert rules and hurts investigations.

q.q: Which data source shows how much traffic moved between two hosts and when, without capturing the contents of the packets?
o: Full packet capture
A packet capture stores the whole packet, including contents.
NetFlow
Right. NetFlow (and IPFIX) records conversation metadata: source, destination, ports, bytes and times.
Application logs
Application logs record what an app did, not network conversations.
Vulnerability scan results
Scans show weaknesses, not traffic.

q.q: A command needs a standard way for tools to check systems against configuration benchmarks and share the results. Which set of standards provides this?
o: SCAP
Right. The Security Content Automation Protocol defines formats so tools can check configurations and vulnerabilities automatically.
SNMP
SNMP monitors and manages network devices, not configuration compliance.
SMTP
SMTP sends email.
SAML
SAML is for single sign-on.

q.q: Which DNS record lets receiving mail servers check whether an email from a domain came from a server the domain authorizes?
o: SPF
Right. Sender Policy Framework lists the servers allowed to send mail for the domain.
DKIM
DKIM adds a digital signature to messages. It proves integrity and origin, but not through an allowed-server list.
MX
MX records say where to deliver mail for a domain, not who may send it.
PTR
A PTR record maps an IP back to a name.

q.q: A domain publishes SPF and DKIM. What does adding DMARC do?
o: Encrypts messages between mail servers so they can't be read
That's TLS (for example STARTTLS) between servers, not DMARC.
Tells receivers how to handle mail that fails SPF and DKIM
Right. DMARC sets the policy (none, quarantine or reject) and sends the domain owner reports on failures.
Lists the servers that are allowed to send mail for the domain
That's SPF.
Adds a digital signature to every outgoing message header
That's DKIM.

q.q: Users keep reaching newly registered phishing domains. Which control can block those lookups before a connection is even made?
o: DNS filtering
Right. DNS filtering refuses to resolve known bad or newly registered risky domains, so the browser never connects.
Full-disk encryption
Encryption doesn't affect web browsing.
Port mirroring
Mirroring copies traffic for monitoring.
A UPS
A UPS provides backup power.

q.q: An EDR tool sees a process encrypting hundreds of files per second on a workstation. What is EDR able to do that traditional antivirus usually can't?
o: Block known malware by matching file signatures
Signature matching is what traditional antivirus already does.
Detect the behavior and isolate the host or kill the process
Right. EDR watches behavior, not just signatures, and can respond automatically.
Quarantine email attachments before users open them
That's an email security gateway's job.
Scan the file share for vulnerable software versions
That's a vulnerability scanner.

q.q: The firewall currently allows inbound TCP 3389 from any source to a group of servers. What is the best change?
o: Leave it open, because RDP traffic is already encrypted
RDP exposed to the internet is one of the most attacked services, encrypted or not.
Remove it and require a VPN or jump server for RDP
Right. RDP should never be open to the internet. Restrict it to a controlled access path.
Keep it but change RDP to a non-standard port
Moving the port only hides it from lazy scans. The service is still exposed.
Keep it but enable account lockout on the servers
Lockout slows guessing but leaves RDP exposed to exploits and spraying.

q.q: A user signs in with a password and then approves a push notification on their phone. Which factors are used?
o: Something you know and something you are
A push approval isn't biometric.
Something you know and something you have
Right. The password is something you know, and the phone is something you have.
Two things you know
The phone isn't a knowledge factor.
Something you have and somewhere you are
Location wasn't checked.

q.q: A member signs in once with their CAC and can then open email, the training portal and the HR system without signing in again. What is this?
o: Single sign-on
Right. SSO lets one authentication grant access to many systems.
Password vaulting
A vault stores and checks out privileged passwords.
Account provisioning
Provisioning creates accounts. It isn't how users sign in.
Time-of-day restrictions
That limits when someone can sign in.

q.q: Access to files is granted based on a user's job function, such as "Yeoman" or "IT2", rather than to each person individually. Which access control model is this?
o: Discretionary access control
In DAC the owner of each file decides who gets access.
Mandatory access control
MAC uses labels and clearances set by the system, not job roles.
Role-based access control
Right. RBAC assigns permissions to roles, and users get them by being in a role.
Rule-based access control
Rule-based access uses conditions such as time or IP, not job roles.

q.q: An admin needs domain admin rights only for a two-hour maintenance task. The access is granted automatically when approved and removed when the window ends. What is this?
o: Just-in-time permissions
Right. JIT access gives elevated rights only when needed and takes them away afterward, shrinking the window an attacker could use.
Permanent privilege
The rights are removed after the task, so they aren't permanent.
Account sharing
Nothing is shared between users.
Federation
Federation lets identities from one organization be trusted by another.

q.q: A member transfers from the Sector to a cutter. Her old access to Sector file shares is never removed, and over several transfers she builds up far more access than her job needs. What is this, and what prevents it?
o: Privilege escalation; patching the file servers
Escalation exploits a flaw to gain rights. Here the rights were granted and never removed.
Privilege creep; access reviews and removal on transfer
Right. Rights pile up when old access isn't removed, so periodic reviews and offboarding steps for transfers are needed.
Role explosion; consolidating the RBAC roles
Too many roles is a design issue, not one person gaining access over time.
Account sharing; unique accounts for every user
Nothing is shared. It's one person's account.

q.q: Which protocol lets a user sign in to a partner organization's web app with their home organization's credentials, by passing an XML assertion?
o: SAML
Right. SAML passes authentication assertions in XML between an identity provider and a service provider for federated SSO.
LDAP
LDAP queries directories, usually within one organization.
RADIUS
RADIUS centralizes network access logins such as VPN and Wi-Fi.
Kerberos
Kerberos uses tickets inside a Windows domain, not XML assertions across organizations.

q.q: A SOC writes a playbook so that when a phishing email is reported, the system automatically pulls the same email from every inbox and blocks the sender. What is the main benefit?
o: It lets the SOC turn off the email gateway
The gateway is still needed for everything that isn't reported.
Faster, consistent response that frees analysts
Right. Automation handles repetitive steps quickly and the same way every time.
It removes the need for analysts to review reports
Automation still needs people to tune it and handle edge cases.
It stops users from receiving phishing at all
No control guarantees that.

q.q: Which is a real risk of heavy security automation?
o: Analysts lose hands-on skills because playbooks do the triage
Skill fade is a real staffing concern, but it isn't the security risk the question is after: errors spreading at machine speed.
A single error in a script can repeat across many systems quickly
Right. Automation multiplies a mistake as fast as it multiplies good work, and complex scripts can become a single point of failure.
Logs stop being created once actions are scripted
Automated actions still generate logs, often more of them.
Users must re-authenticate every time a playbook runs
Playbooks run under service accounts. They don't force users to sign in again.

q.q: A SOC confirms ransomware on three workstations. What should the team do next, according to the incident response process?
o: Restore the three workstations from last night's backup
Recovery comes after containment and eradication, or the ransomware may hit the restored systems.
Isolate the affected workstations to contain the spread
Right. After detection and analysis, containment stops the spread before eradication and recovery.
Start the lessons-learned review while details are fresh
Lessons learned is the final phase, after the incident is resolved.
Reimage every computer in the unit as a precaution
That's far beyond what's needed, and it isn't containment.

q.q: An investigator copies a suspect drive. Which step proves the copy is identical to the original and hasn't been changed?
o: Compare cryptographic hashes of the original and the copy
Right. Matching hashes show the image is an exact copy, which supports integrity in court.
Open the files to check that they look the same
Opening files can change metadata and doesn't prove every bit matches.
Record the drive's serial number
The serial number identifies the drive, not the integrity of the copy.
Encrypt the copy
Encryption protects confidentiality, not proof of a matching copy.

q.q: Evidence from a breach is handed from the responder to the legal office. What document records who had it, when and why?
o: Chain of custody
Right. Chain of custody tracks every handoff so the evidence holds up later.
Legal hold notice
A legal hold tells people to keep relevant data. It doesn't track handoffs.
Incident response plan
The IR plan describes the process, not a specific evidence trail.
Non-disclosure agreement
An NDA restricts sharing information.

q.q: Analysts search the network for signs of an attacker that hasn't triggered any alerts, based on a hypothesis about a known adversary's techniques. What is this?
o: Threat hunting
Right. Threat hunting is proactive: analysts look for hidden threats instead of waiting for alerts.
Penetration testing
Pen testing tries to break in, not find someone already inside.
Vulnerability scanning
Scanning looks for weaknesses, not active attackers.
Tabletop exercise
A tabletop discusses a scenario on paper.

q.q: An analyst needs to know exactly which commands an attacker sent to a compromised web server over an unencrypted connection. Which data source shows this best?
o: A packet capture of the traffic
Right. A full packet capture shows the actual contents of unencrypted traffic, including the commands.
NetFlow records
NetFlow shows that the hosts talked and how much, not what was said.
The DHCP lease log
DHCP logs show IP assignments.
The vulnerability scan report
A scan report shows weaknesses, not commands sent.

q.q: A phishing email is reported. Which part of it helps an analyst trace the mail servers it passed through?
o: The email headers
Right. Headers record each server hop, timestamps and authentication results such as SPF and DKIM.
The subject line
The subject is set by the sender and is easy to fake.
The signature block
Signature text is easy to fake.
The display name
The display name can be anything the sender types.

q.q: Which TWO log sources would best show whether a user's workstation ran a suspicious PowerShell script? (Choose two.)
o: Endpoint (EDR) logs
Right. EDR records process launches and command lines on the host.
Windows operating system event logs, including PowerShell logging
Right. Windows can log script blocks and process creation when those logs are turned on.
Firewall logs
Firewall logs show network connections, not which script ran.
Badge reader logs
Badge logs show who entered a building.
DHCP logs
DHCP logs show which IP a device got.

q.q: Which information in a photo's metadata could help an investigation into where and when it was taken?
o: The file's creation date in the file system
File-system dates change when files are copied, so they're less reliable than embedded metadata.
EXIF data such as GPS coordinates and time
Right. EXIF metadata can include the camera, time and location the photo was taken.
The image's resolution and color depth
These describe the image quality, not where or when it was taken.
The hash value of the image file
A hash identifies the exact file but says nothing about time or place.

q.q: Which document gives mandatory, specific technical requirements, such as "all laptops must use AES-256 full-disk encryption"?
o: Policy
A policy states high-level intent, such as "protect sensitive data," without the technical detail.
Standard
Right. Standards set mandatory, specific requirements that support a policy.
Guideline
Guidelines are recommendations, not requirements.
Procedure
A procedure gives step-by-step instructions for doing a task.

q.q: Which role is responsible for deciding how a dataset is classified and who should have access to it?
o: Data custodian
The custodian handles day-to-day care, such as backups and storage, following the owner's decisions.
Data owner
Right. The data owner, usually a senior leader, is accountable for classification and access decisions.
Data processor
A processor handles data on behalf of a controller, such as a vendor running payroll.
Data subject
The subject is the person the data is about.

q.q: A board of senior leaders meets quarterly to approve security policies and set priorities across the organization. What is this?
o: A change advisory board
A CAB approves technical changes, not organization-wide security policy.
A governance board or security committee
Right. Boards and committees are governance structures that set direction and approve policy.
A computer incident response team
An IR team handles incidents, not policy approval.
A security operations center
A SOC monitors and responds to threats day to day.

q.q: Which document gives the exact steps a help desk technician follows to reset a user's password safely?
o: Procedure
Right. Procedures are step-by-step instructions for a specific task.
Policy
A policy is high-level and doesn't list steps.
Standard
A standard sets requirements, not the steps.
Guideline
A guideline offers advice that's optional.

q.q: An organization's acceptable use policy (AUP) is mainly meant to:
o: Explain how users report a suspected incident
Reporting steps belong in an incident procedure, though an AUP may point to them.
Define what users may and may not do on the systems
Right. The AUP sets the rules users agree to, so misuse can be addressed.
Set the technical requirements for passwords
Password requirements belong in a standard.
Describe how user accounts are created and removed
That's an account management procedure.

q.q: A server worth $50,000 would lose 40% of its value in a flood. Floods are expected once every 10 years. What is the annualized loss expectancy (ALE)?
o: That's the single loss expectancy, the loss from one flood.
That would be the full value times the ARO, ignoring the exposure factor.
That multiplies by 10 instead of dividing.

q.q: A unit buys cyber insurance to cover the cost of a data breach. Which risk strategy is this?
o: Avoid
Avoiding means stopping the risky activity altogether.
Mitigate
Mitigating means lowering the likelihood or impact with controls.
Transfer
Right. Insurance shifts the financial impact to another party.
Accept
Accepting means taking the risk as is, with no action.

q.q: A command decides to stop offering a public file upload feature because the risk can't be reduced to an acceptable level. Which strategy is this?
o: Avoid
Right. Ending the activity removes the risk entirely.
Transfer
Nothing is moved to another party.
Accept
They aren't keeping the feature and living with the risk.
Mitigate
Mitigating would keep the feature with added controls.

q.q: Where does an organization record each identified risk, its owner, its rating and the planned response?
o: Risk register
Right. The risk register tracks risks, owners, ratings, responses and status.
Asset inventory
An inventory lists assets, not risks.
Change log
A change log records changes made to systems.
Firewall rule base
That's technical configuration.

q.q: Leadership states that it will accept no more than low risk for systems that handle personnel data. What does this statement define?
o: Residual risk
Residual risk is what's left after controls are applied.
Risk appetite
Right. Risk appetite (and tolerance) describes how much risk the organization is willing to accept.
Inherent risk
Inherent risk is the risk before any controls.
Risk threshold breach
A breach of a threshold is when risk goes over the limit, not the statement setting it.

q.q: After installing new controls, some risk remains. What is that remaining risk called?
o: Inherent risk
Inherent risk is the level before controls.
Residual risk
Right. Residual risk is what's left after controls, and leadership decides whether to accept it.
Control risk
Control risk is the chance a control fails to work.
Zero risk
Risk is never zero.

q.q: Which analysis identifies how long each mission function can be down, and what an outage would cost, so recovery priorities can be set?
o: Business impact analysis
Right. A BIA finds critical functions, the impact of losing them and recovery targets like RTO and RPO.
Vulnerability scan
A scan finds technical weaknesses.
Penetration test
A pen test tries to break in.
Gap analysis
A gap analysis compares current controls with a standard.

q.q: A risk assessment rates risks as High, Medium or Low based on team judgment rather than dollar values. What kind of assessment is this?
o: Quantitative
Quantitative uses numbers, such as SLE, ARO and ALE in dollars.
Qualitative
Right. Qualitative assessment uses ratings and judgment rather than exact figures.
Continuous
Continuous describes how often you assess, not the method.
One-time
One-time describes how often, not the method.

q.q: Before signing with a new cloud email vendor, the command reviews the vendor's independent SOC 2 Type II report and security questionnaire. What is this step?
o: A penetration test of the vendor
You usually can't test a vendor's systems without their written permission and scope.
Vendor assessment as part of due diligence
Right. Reviewing a vendor's security evidence before signing is third-party risk assessment.
Supply chain analysis of the vendor's software
Supply chain analysis looks at components and suppliers. The step described is reviewing the vendor's own audit.
Ongoing vendor monitoring
Monitoring happens after the contract starts. This is before signing.

q.q: Which agreement defines measurable service levels, such as 99.9% uptime, and what happens if the vendor misses them?
o: SLA
Right. A service-level agreement sets measurable performance targets and penalties.
NDA
An NDA protects confidential information.
MOU
An MOU records a general understanding, usually without binding service levels.
BPA
A business partners agreement sets out how partners share profits, losses and responsibilities.

q.q: A contract lets the unit review a vendor's security controls and records on request. Which clause is this?
o: Right-to-audit clause
Right. A right-to-audit clause gives the customer permission to inspect the vendor's controls.
Non-compete clause
That limits working for competitors.
Indemnification clause
That decides who pays for certain losses.
Force majeure clause
That excuses performance during events outside anyone's control.

q.q: A sector and a state agency agree to run a joint port-security task force. They need a document that spells out each side's specific responsibilities and is more binding than a simple statement of shared intent. Which fits best?
o: Memorandum of agreement (MOA)
Right. An MOA sets out specific responsibilities each party agrees to, and is more formal than an MOU.
Memorandum of understanding (MOU)
An MOU records a shared intent or understanding and usually isn't binding on specific duties.
Non-disclosure agreement (NDA)
An NDA only covers keeping information confidential.
Service-level agreement (SLA)
An SLA sets measurable service targets for a provider, not shared task-force duties.

q.q: A unit discovers it has been storing members' SSNs in a spreadsheet on an open share for a year. Which consequences of non-compliance could follow?
o: A finding that only affects the unit's IT budget
Privacy failures carry legal and reputational effects, not only budget ones.
Fines, sanctions and reputational damage
Right. Non-compliance with privacy rules can bring fines, sanctions, contract impacts and reputational harm.
Loss of the unit's ATO for every system it runs
An ATO is per system. A spreadsheet on a share doesn't automatically revoke every authorization.
A requirement to rebuild the network from scratch
Rebuilding the network wouldn't fix a data handling failure.

q.q: Under privacy law, which party decides why and how personal data is processed?
o: Data controller
Right. The controller sets the purpose and means of processing and is accountable for it.
Data processor
A processor acts on the controller's instructions.
Data subject
The subject is the person the data is about.
Data custodian
A custodian takes care of the data technically.

q.q: A member asks the command to delete personal data it no longer needs. Which privacy concept does this request reflect?
o: Data sovereignty
Sovereignty is about the laws that apply where data is stored.
The right to be forgotten
Right. The right to be forgotten (erasure) lets a person ask for their data to be deleted where it isn't needed.
Data minimization
Minimization limits what's collected in the first place. This request is about deleting data already held.
Data retention
Retention sets how long data is kept. The request is to remove it.

q.q: A command reports its security posture to higher headquarters each quarter, as required by policy. What is this an example of?
o: Internal audit
An internal audit is a review by the organization's own auditors, not a report to an outside authority.
External compliance reporting
Right. Reporting to an outside authority shows the organization is meeting its requirements.
Continuous monitoring
Monitoring produces data for the report, but the act described is the reporting itself.
Attestation of controls
Attestation is an independent party confirming controls, not the unit's own report.

q.q: A pen tester is given full network diagrams, source code and admin credentials before the test. What kind of test is this?
o: Known environment (white box)
Right. With full information, the tester can test thoroughly in less time.
Unknown environment (black box)
In an unknown environment test the tester gets no inside information.
Partially known environment (gray box)
Gray box gives some information, not everything.
Passive reconnaissance
Passive recon gathers public information without touching the target.

q.q: Before a penetration test begins, what must be agreed in writing to define what the testers may do?
o: A signed non-disclosure agreement
An NDA keeps findings confidential, but it doesn't define what the testers are allowed to do.
Rules of engagement with scope and authorization
Right. The rules of engagement set scope, timing, methods and permission. Without them, testing can be illegal.
A statement of work listing deliverables
A SOW covers deliverables and cost, but scope and permission belong in the rules of engagement.
The unit's incident response plan
The IR plan is for real incidents, not for authorizing a test.

q.q: An outside firm reviews the unit's controls and issues a formal opinion that they're designed and working as stated. What is that formal statement called?
o: Attestation
Right. Attestation is an independent party formally confirming that controls meet stated requirements.
Self-assessment
A self-assessment is done internally.
Reconnaissance
Reconnaissance gathers information about a target.
Tabletop exercise
A tabletop discusses a scenario.

q.q: Which TWO are passive reconnaissance activities a pen tester might do first? (Choose two.)
o: Searching public records and social media about the organization
Right. OSINT gathers information without touching the target's systems.
Looking up the organization's DNS records and websites like any visitor
Right. Viewing public information as any user would doesn't probe the target actively.
Running a port scan against the public IP range
A port scan sends packets to the target, which is active reconnaissance.
Trying default passwords on the VPN
