That's an active attack attempt.
Sending a phishing email to staff
That's active social engineering.

q.q: The command sends a fake phishing email to all hands and tracks who clicks and who reports it. What is the main goal?
o: Find which users should lose email access
Simulations are for learning, not punishment.
Measure and improve how users spot and report phishing
Right. Simulations show who needs more training and build the habit of reporting.
Test whether the spam filter blocks phishing
Simulations are usually allow-listed through the filter on purpose, so they test people, not the filter.
Check that MFA prompts appear on every sign-in
A phishing simulation doesn't test MFA prompts.

q.q: A sailor notices a colleague logging in at odd hours and copying large amounts of data to removable media. What should the sailor do?
o: Ask the colleague directly what they're copying
Confronting them could tip off a real insider and destroy evidence.
Report it through the unit's security reporting channel
Right. Recognizing and reporting unusual behavior is a key part of security awareness.
Wait to see if it happens again before saying anything
Waiting gives a real insider more time to take data.
Unplug the colleague's workstation from the network
That isn't the sailor's role and may destroy evidence.

q.q: Which training topic best prepares remote workers for the risks of working from a coffee shop?
o: Locking the laptop to the table with a cable lock at all times
Cable locks help against theft, but the bigger daily risks in a coffee shop are untrusted Wi-Fi and shoulder surfing.
Using the VPN on public Wi-Fi and keeping screens out of view
Right. Remote work training covers secure connections and privacy in public places.
Turning off the laptop firewall so the café network works
Disabling the firewall on an untrusted network raises risk.
Sharing a hotspot with coworkers to save cellular data
Sharing a hotspot doesn't address the risks of working in public and can expose others.

q.title: Set the firewall rules for a new boat station network
q.scenario: A boat station has a LAN (10.20.10.0/24), a server VLAN with a file server (10.20.30.5) and a DNS resolver (10.20.30.53), and an internet connection. Configure each rule so it meets the requirement. Rules run top to bottom.

rows.req: LAN users can open shared folders on the file server.
rows.why: File sharing is SMB on TCP 445, from the LAN subnet to the file server only.

rows.req: LAN users can resolve names through the station's DNS resolver.
rows.why: DNS lookups use UDP 53, from the LAN to the resolver.

rows.req: Nobody can manage devices with Telnet, which sends passwords in clear text.
rows.why: Telnet (TCP 23) is unencrypted, so deny it from any source to any destination and use SSH instead.

rows.req: LAN users can browse secure websites.
rows.why: HTTPS is TCP 443, from the LAN to any destination on the internet.

rows.req: Block everything not explicitly allowed above.
rows.why: The implicit deny goes last. Placed first, it would block every rule below it.

q.title: Name the attack in each event
q.scenario: The SOC flagged five events. Pick the attack each one shows. Each answer is used once; two options are distractors.

items.log:
Logon type 3  account: CG\dadmin  auth: NTLM  src: 10.20.10.44
... same account, 31 servers, 0301 to 0305, no interactive logon ...
items.why: One admin account authenticating with NTLM to many servers in minutes, with no password typed, points to a reused hash.
Encoded ../ sequences (%2F is /) climb out of the web folder to read a system file.

items.log:
0200-0230  1 failed sign-in each for 412 accounts
all from 198.51.100.7  password hash identical across attempts
items.why: One password, tried once per account across many accounts, is spraying. It avoids lockouts.

items.text: Several users typed the correct intranet address but landed on a look-alike login page. The site's real IP hasn't changed, but the local resolver returns a different one.
items.why: The right name resolving to the wrong IP at the resolver means the DNS cache was poisoned.
Script saved into a forum post runs for every reader and sends their cookies away: stored XSS.

q.title: Put each action in its incident response phase
q.scenario: A cutter's network had a malware outbreak. The actions below are listed out of order. For each one, pick the incident response phase it belongs to. Each phase is used once; one option is a distractor.

items.text: The team built jump kits and practiced a tabletop exercise last quarter.
items.why: Training, tools and plans made before an incident are preparation.

items.text: The EDR raised an alert for a process encrypting files on two workstations.
items.why: Noticing that something may be wrong is detection.

items.text: Analysts confirmed the alert was real, identified the malware family and its scope.
items.why: Validating the alert and working out what happened and how far it spread is analysis.

items.text: The two workstations were moved to an isolated VLAN.
The malware and its persistence registry keys were removed and passwords reset.
items.why: Removing the threat from the environment is eradication.

items.text: Cleaned systems were restored from known-good images and returned to service with extra monitoring.
items.why: Bringing systems back to normal operation is recovery.

items.text: The team met to review what worked, what didn't and which controls to add.
items.why: The after-action review is lessons learned.

q.title: Choose a risk response for each finding
q.scenario: The risk register has five open items. For each one, pick the response that best fits the decision described.

rows.req: A breach of the member database could cost far more than the unit's budget. The command buys a cyber insurance policy.
rows.why: Insurance shifts the financial impact to another party: transfer.

rows.req: An old public upload portal keeps getting attacked and isn't needed any more. It's shut down.
rows.why: Stopping the activity removes the risk: avoid.

rows.req: Phishing is the top threat. The unit adds MFA and email filtering.
rows.why: Controls that lower likelihood or impact: mitigate.

rows.req: A training lab server holds no sensitive data, and fixing a low-severity finding would cost more than any possible loss. Leadership signs off on leaving it.
rows.why: A formal decision to live with a low risk: accept.

rows.req: Laptops are often lost on deployments. Full-disk encryption is enforced on every laptop.
rows.why: Encryption reduces the impact of a lost laptop: mitigate.

q.title: Pick the right protection for each need
q.scenario: Each request below needs one protection method. Pick the best fit for each.

rows.req: Prove a downloaded installer hasn't been changed since the vendor published it, by comparing a value.
rows.why: Comparing a published hash with your own shows the file is unchanged.

rows.req: Prove a memo really came from the CO and that the CO can't deny sending it.
rows.why: A signature made with the CO's private key gives integrity, authenticity and non-repudiation.

rows.req: Keep a lost laptop's files unreadable.
rows.why: Full-disk encryption protects everything on the drive when the device is off or stolen.

rows.req: Protect member data as it travels between the browser and the portal.
rows.why: TLS encrypts data in transit.

rows.req: Let the help desk see only the last four digits of an account number.
rows.why: Masking hides part of the value from people who don't need it.

rows.req: Store a stand-in value for card numbers that can't be reversed mathematically.
rows.why: Tokenization swaps in a random token and keeps the real value in a secure vault.

q.title: Classify the access controls
q.scenario: For each situation, pick the access control model it describes and the authentication factor in use, if any.

rows.req: Files are opened only by people whose clearance label is equal to or higher than the file's label. Users enter a PIN at the door.
rows.why: Labels and clearances set by the system are MAC. A PIN is something you know.

rows.req: All Yeomen get the personnel share because of their job. They sign in with a fingerprint.
rows.why: Access by job role is RBAC. A fingerprint is something you are.

rows.req: The owner of a team folder decides who else may open it. Access is via a smart card.
rows.why: Owner-granted access is DAC. A smart card is something you have.

rows.req: Access is allowed only if the user is in the Engineering department, on a managed device and connecting from a US IP address.
rows.why: Decisions based on several attributes are ABAC. The US IP check is somewhere you are.

rows.req: The VPN refuses all connections between 2200 and 0500, for everyone.
rows.why: A blanket condition that applies to everyone is rule-based. No user factor is involved.

q.title: Find the attack in the VPN gateway log
q.scenario: The SIEM raised an alert on the VPN gateway. Read the log, mark every line that belongs to the attack, then say what it shows.
q.ticket: SIEM alert #4471: possible account takeover on vpn-gw01 between 02:00 and 02:45.

lines.text: 02:14:07 sshd[2210]: Failed password for invalid user admin from 203.0.113.50 port 51122 ssh2
lines.why: Many failed logins for names that do not exist, all from one outside address, is a password-guessing run.

lines.text: 02:14:09 sshd[2212]: Failed password for invalid user test from 203.0.113.50 port 51124 ssh2
lines.why: Same source, a new made-up user name two seconds later. Part of the same guessing run.

lines.text: 02:14:12 sshd[2215]: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.50 port 51127 ssh2
lines.why: The attacker is now trying the root account. Still the same run.

lines.text: 02:20:41 sshd[2301]: Accepted publickey for gdavis from 10.20.10.44 port 49802 ssh2
lines.why: A key-based login from the internal admin workstation. This is normal.

lines.text: 02:21:03 sudo: gdavis : TTY=pts/0 ; COMMAND=/usr/bin/systemctl status sshd
lines.why: A real admin checking the SSH service. Not suspicious on its own.

lines.text: 02:31:55 sshd[2388]: Accepted password for root from 203.0.113.50 port 51390 ssh2
lines.why: A success from the attacking address after the failures. This is the moment the attacker got in.

lines.text: 02:32:10 useradd[2402]: new user: name=svc-backup2, UID=0, GID=0, shell=/bin/bash
lines.why: A new account with UID 0 has full root power. Attackers create these as a hidden way back in.

ask.label: What does this log show?
opts: Password guessing, then a backdoor account
ask.why: Guessing, then a successful login, then a new root-level account to keep access: brute force followed by persistence.

q.title: Spot the web attack in the access log
q.scenario: The web server's response sizes look odd this morning. Mark every request that is part of an attack, then name the attack.
q.ticket: Ticket #5120: the public product page returned a 48 KB response where it usually returns about 3 KB.

lines.why: A staff computer loading the home page. Normal.
By itself this is a normal product page request. What matters is what the same address does next.
A lone quote added to the value, and the server answered with an error. Attackers do this to test whether input reaches the database.
OR 1=1 is always true, so the query returned the whole table. That is the 48 KB response in the ticket.
UNION SELECT glues a second query onto the page's query to read the users table. Clear sign of SQL injection.
The admin workstation logging in. Normal.
A staff computer loading the contact page. Normal.
The same address now hunts for a database backup file. A 404 means it was not there, but it is still part of the attack.

ask.label: Which attack is this?
ask.why: Quotes, OR 1=1 and UNION SELECT typed into a URL value are classic SQL injection. Fix: parameterized queries plus input validation.

q.title: Build the guest Wi-Fi firewall rule set
q.scenario: Guests may browse the web. Guests must never reach the server VLAN. Staff keep file-share access. Everything else is blocked.
q.ticket: Change request CR-1182. Guest Wi-Fi is 10.20.50.0/24, the server VLAN is 10.20.30.0/24 (file server 10.20.30.5), staff LAN is 10.20.10.0/24.

rules.why: This is the rule that keeps guests out of the server VLAN.
Lets guests browse the web. It must sit below the deny rule, or guests could reach the servers over web ports too.
Staff file-share access (SMB), limited to the one file server.
A default deny blocks everything not allowed above.
Allows everything, which cancels every restriction. It never belongs in a least-privilege rule set.
Opens Remote Desktop on the file server to the whole Internet. Nobody asked for it and it is very risky.

before.why: Rules run top to bottom and the first match wins. The guest deny must come before the broad web allow.

last.why: Anything below a match-everything rule never runs, so the default deny must be last.

q.title: Cut off an infected kiosk and keep the rest working
q.scenario: One lobby kiosk is infected. Quarantine it without breaking the rest of the staff network. Rules run top to bottom.
q.ticket: Incident 7003. Kiosk 10.20.10.99 is beaconing to the Internet. Staff LAN is 10.20.10.0/24 and needs HTTPS out. Only the admin workstation 10.20.10.44 may SSH to the switch network 10.20.60.0/24.

rules.why: Cuts the infected kiosk off from everything.
Keeps normal HTTPS browsing working for the rest of the LAN.
Lets only the admin workstation manage the switches.
Would undo the quarantine and every other restriction.
Telnet sends passwords in clear text, and this would open it to everyone. Never allow it.

before.why: The kiosk is inside 10.20.10.0/24, so the broad HTTPS allow would let it through if it came first. The specific deny must be above it.

last.why: The cleanup deny matches everything, so it has to be the last rule.

q.title: Stop the SSH attack on web01
q.scenario: Find the address that is attacking SSH on web01 and block it with the firewall. Then check that the block is active. Do not block the admin workstation, 10.20.10.44.
q.ticket: IDS alert: hundreds of failed SSH logins on web01 in ten minutes.

checks.t: Read the failed logins in the auth log
checks.why: SSH logins are recorded in auth.log. Searching it shows who is being guessed at, and from which address.
One outside address caused almost every failure. A firewall deny stops it right away (containment).

checks.t: Did not block the admin workstation 10.20.10.44
checks.why: That address is a trusted admin who made one typo. Blocking it would be an outage you caused yourself.

checks.t: Checked the firewall after the change
checks.why: Always verify that a change took effect. The firewall status shows the new deny rule in the list.

q.title: Close an old Telnet service without locking yourself out
q.scenario: A scan found Telnet listening on a server. Find it, shut it down so it stays off after a reboot, and confirm it is closed. Keep SSH running: it is your only way in.
q.ticket: Vulnerability scan finding: port 23/tcp open on files01 (Telnet sends passwords in clear text).
q.intro: files01 (Debian 12). Type help to see the commands.

cmds.out:
State   Local Address:Port  Process
LISTEN  0.0.0.0:22          sshd
LISTEN  0.0.0.0:23          systemd (telnet.socket)
LISTEN  0.0.0.0:445         smbd

alt.out:
State   Local Address:Port  Process
LISTEN  0.0.0.0:22          sshd
LISTEN  0.0.0.0:445         smbd

cmds.out: (no output) Your SSH session just dropped. You are locked out.

checks.why: Look before you change anything. The listening-ports list shows what is actually exposed.
Stopping the service closes the port. A firewall deny also blocks it, but the service would still be running.

checks.t: Telnet is disabled so it stays off after a reboot
checks.why: Stopping a service only lasts until the next reboot. Disabling it removes it from startup.
SSH is the encrypted way to manage the server. Stopping it would lock you out.

checks.t: Checked again that port 23 is closed
checks.why: Verify the result. After the change the listening list should no longer show port 23.

q.title: Place the devices in the boat-station network
q.scenario: The station runs a public website and an internal file server. Place each device where it belongs. Two devices in the tray are not needed.

devs.name: Firewall
devs.why: A firewall belongs at the edge. Everything from the Internet must pass through it first.

devs.name: Web server
devs.why: Public servers sit in the DMZ, so a break-in does not land on the inside LAN.

devs.name: File server
devs.why: Internal data stays on the inside LAN, behind the firewall and away from the public.

devs.name: Hub
devs.why: A hub just repeats traffic to every port and adds no security. It has no job in this design.

devs.name: Open Wi-Fi AP
devs.why: An open access point would be a back door around the firewall.

q.title: Place the devices for secure remote access
q.scenario: Staff work from home over a VPN, the public portal sits behind a reverse proxy, and security logs go to one place. Put each device in its right spot. Two are not needed.

slots.label: Spot B
slots.hint: sits in front of the public portal

devs.name: VPN gateway
devs.why: Remote staff reach the network through one hardened entry point at the edge, not through random open ports.

devs.name: Reverse proxy
devs.why: It takes public web requests in the DMZ and passes only clean ones on, so the portal itself is never exposed directly.

devs.name: RADIUS server
devs.why: The authentication server stays on the inside LAN where the Internet cannot reach it.

devs.name: Log collector (SIEM)
devs.why: Logs go to a separate management network so an attacker who breaks into a server cannot erase them.

devs.name: Hub
devs.why: A hub adds no filtering or logging. It has no job in this design.

devs.name: Old router, default password
devs.why: A device with a default password is an easy way in. Never add one to a secure design.
